markupAndEmbeds.html: Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, today described the historic Democratic sweep in the midterm elections as an “ass-kicking” for Republicans, urging the party to deliver on economic promises in the next cycle.
“It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election, it was a Watergate-level repudiation,” Cruz said on an episode of his podcast, describing the Democratic shift across the country as a “blue tsunami.”
Cruz, who is not up for re-election until 2030, said that “understandably, people were pissed off,” as “Republicans didn’t do enough to address their very real pain.”
He pointed to tariffs’ raising costs and the Iran war’s dragging on for “too long,” adding, “Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high.”

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani told NBC News today that last night’s wins “absolutely” pave the way for a progressive candidate in the 2028 presidential race.

Speaking with Kristen Welker on "Meet the Press NOW," Mamdani claimed the victories by Sen.-elect James Talarico, D-Texas; Sen.-elect Annie Andrews, D-S.C.; and Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, D-Ga., as wins for the progressive movement, saying their campaigns bore the “hallmarks of what progressive governance” looks like.
Mamdani also responded to Vice President JD Vance's blaming the Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.
“This is a war that they started; it’s a war that they can end. If they think it was part of their political demise, why don’t they take some action to reflect that?” Mamdani said.
While he dodged the question of impeachment, Mamdani said he supports “Congress taking action to confront the corruption that we have seen in Washington.”

He also reaffirmed his support for House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., in leadership positions but stopped short of encouraging candidates he backed to support them as the top Democrats in the next Congress.

Connie Chan today conceded to fellow Democrat Scott Wiener in California’s 11th Congressional District, where the winner will succeed Democratic Rep. Nancy Pelosi, the former House speaker.

“After reviewing the results and the ballots remaining to be counted, while we expect the margin to narrow significantly, we do not have a clear path to victory,” Chan wrote in a statement. “I congratulate Scott Wiener on his election and wish him success in serving San Francisco.”
NBC News has not yet projected a winner in the race. Pelosi endorsed Chan, a San Francisco Board of Supervisors member, in May.

“I am deeply grateful to Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi for her trust and for four decades of extraordinary service that have strengthened San Francisco and our country. Her incomparable legacy is secure, and it was an honor to have earned her support,” Chan wrote today.

Billionaire Leon Black filed a defamation lawsuit today against Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, which has spearheaded a Jeffrey Epstein investigation.
Black has been the target of subpoenas from the Republican-led committee, which unanimously voted in September to hold him in contempt over his refusal to comply with those subpoenas.

Black, a former Wall Street private equity investor who had a business relationship with Epstein, sued Garcia in the Southern District of New York, alleging he “has knowingly and willfully lied about Leon Black and defamed him.” The suit cites comments from Garcia that Black was “at the center” and “directly involved” with Epstein’s crimes.

A spokesperson for Garcia didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit. Garcia said in a statement in September in response to a lawsuit Black filed against the committee that Black had “funded Epstein’s abuse and trafficking of women,” adding: “Multiple women have also accused Black of sexual assault. His connections to Epstein and his unwillingness to cooperate are unacceptable.”
Read the full story here.

They didn’t have much to work with.
The president’s party almost always loses ground in midterms, and Trump’s record offered few promising angles for reversing that curse.

After a historic wave of Democratic victories last night, Trump today pressed the Senate to pass a bill that would make daylight saving time permanent when it returns to session.

"Too bad the Senate has not yet approved the Sunshine Protection Act or, the I Don’t Want to Change My Clocks Anymore Act," Trump wrote on Truth Social. "I didn’t want to make a big deal out of this prior to the Election because I didn’t want to have certain Senators lose their Race, in a landslide, but it is too bad they can’t get it done."

The House passed the bill in July, but the Senate has failed to get it over the finish line. It has faced opposition from several GOP senators, including Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and Tom Cotton of Arkansas, Mike Rounds of South Dakota, Steve Daines of Montana, Todd Young of Indiana and Bernie Moreno of Ohio.
Cotton and Rounds both won re-election, NBC News projects. Daines withdrew his re-election bid this year, and Thune, Young and Moreno were not up for re-election this year.
Trump complained today that "it's so dark outside, so early," and added that "everyone’s been running around changing their clocks all over the place."
"We have far bigger priorities, but I will keep fighting for this!" he wrote.
Since Congress has not yet approved the Sunshine Protection Act, clocks did fall back an hour Sunday in all states except Hawaii and most of Arizona.

Democrat Allison Montgomery unseated GOP state lawmaker Phillip Rigsby last night to become Alabama's first transgender lawmaker in a district that has voted for Trump three times.

"I know the headlines tomorrow are gonna be provocative and catchy, but let's focus on the most important part of this victory: we showed that a truly grassroots campaign that stands on its policies and its principles has a real shot in Alabama," Montgomery said in a statement.

Montgomery will represent Alabama House District 25, which includes areas in Madison and Limestone counties. Trump won those counties by 9 and 43 percentage points, respectively, in 2024. He also won in both places in 2020 and 2016.

"I'm going to work especially hard for those who hate me, because they deserve a better Alabama as much as anyone," Montgomery said. "We the people are tired of attempts to distract us with culture war issues, whether we’re in a minority group or not."

Rigsby told voters during the campaign that they should be concerned by Montgomery's ability to govern since she is transgender, saying that once somebody transitions, it changes "how they approach things, how they look at policy and how they move legislation."
Montgomery has denounced that characerization, saying Rigsby was trying to "distract" voters from real issues.

Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin predicted today that Hakeem Jeffries’ and Chuck Schumer’s leadership in Congress will be just fine.

“Democrats, we made a lot of promises during this campaign, and we have to deliver on them, and I know Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer are committed to doing that,” Martin said in an interview with Fox News’ Bret Baier.
Asked whether he thinks Jeffries and Schumer will continue to be the Democratic leaders of the House and the Senate, respectively, Martin said yes.
“I have no reason to believe they won’t be,” Martin said. “They’ve done an excellent job with the campaigns, recruiting exceptional candidates and winning.”

Asked about opposition to his leadership from new members today, Schumer, D-N.Y., said the issue “is not for me” and added he will be re-elected as majority leader. Jeffries, D-N.Y., meanwhile, sent out a letter to colleagues officially launching his bid for House speaker, which no members have challenged as of now.

Several candidates pledged not to back Schumer for leader during their campaigns. One of the new members, Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, didn’t commit to back him in an interview this morning with NBC’s “TODAY” show.
“We need action,” El-Sayed said. “We need leadership toward that action. And I’m interested to see, working with the rest of our caucus, what options we’ve got.”

A House race in Louisiana’s redrawn 5th Congressional District will head to a runoff between a Democrat and a Republican after no candidate met the required 50% threshold to win.
Democrat Patricia Moore, who leads with 17.9% of the vote, will go up against Republican Gabe Firment, who is closely behind her at 17.2%. They will face off Dec. 12.
The race included six Republicans and three Democrats. Republican candidates cumulatively earned 63.8% of the votes cast.
The district is currently represented by Republican Sen.-elect Julia Letlow.

Louisiana did not hold primary elections for House seats this year. Republican Gov. Jeff Landry opted to suspend them, even though tens of thousands of votes had already been cast, after the Supreme Court further weakened the Voting Rights Act by finding that the existing map in Louisiana was an unconstitutional racial gerrymander.
As a result, all candidates regardless of party competed in this year’s House general elections.
